Modern.brandNameRationale: The exposed brick wall is the universal stand-up backdrop — codified by the early Comedy Cellar and Catch a Rising Star rooms in 1970s–80s New York, then copied everywhere. Naming the club for the backdrop puts the room itself, not the brand, at the front.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern comedy clubs compete on lineup and design polish. There is room for a club whose entire visual identity is the backdrop the audience already knows — exposed brick, low ceiling, a single mic.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Comedy Cellar (comedycellar.com) holds the canonical New York reference (TM). Helium Comedy Club (heliumcomedy.com) is the modern circuit peer. Caroline's (carolines.com) is the institutional precedent. We sit closer to Comedy Cellar in posture, smaller in footprint.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern comedy room built around the brick wall and a single mic.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Goes to a show once a month. Reads the lineup before buying. Will travel across town for a comic they've seen on a podcast.
behaviors: Reads the lineup before the night
Tips the server, not the comic

dos: Show the lineup and the times
Photograph the room, not the comic
Print the two-drink minimum on the ticket

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only — BRICKWALL set in a tight modern grotesk, all caps, with a small running-bond brick pattern as the favicon.

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and lineups
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for showtimes and prices
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the showtimes, the regular carries the room.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Catch a Rising Star (NYC, 1972) was the room where Letterman, Seinfeld, Larry David, and a generation of stand-ups were first booked. Rising Star Room places the brand in that lineage as a small heritage booking room, without using the active mark.
Luxury.industrySummary: Heritage stand-up rooms are a small segment dominated by a handful of legacy clubs. There is room for a small new room with a heritage register — a 75-seat booking-led venue with a strict guest list and a printed program.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: The Stand (thestandnyc.com) holds the modern heritage-booking slot. Largo at the Coronet (largo-la.com) is the considered-room peer. The Comedy Cellar (comedycellar.com) is the institutional reference (TM). We sit closer to Largo in posture, smaller in seat count.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A 75-seat heritage booking room in the New York 1970s tradition.

targetAudience.primary: 35 to 65. Has been going to comedy shows for thirty years. Knows the bookers by name. Pays for the table by the stage.
behaviors: Books a table for the early show

dos: Print the program on heavy paper
donts: Photograph the comic in the green room

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Rising Star Room set in a high-contrast classical serif, with a small five-point star as the hallmark, foiled in brass on the program cover.

typography.primary: Adobe Jenson for the wordmark and program
typography.secondary: Söhne for the website and ticket portal
typography.rationale: Jenson carries the heritage register. Söhne handles the booking confirmation.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: The mic drop is the gesture at the end of the set — the comic walks off, leaves the mic, the room laughs. Naming the company for the exit moment frames the brand around the punchline rather than the venue.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimal comedy brands are rare — the category leans loud. There is room for a small touring-show operator whose entire identity is the close: tight 60-minute sets, no opener, no MC announcement, end on the line.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Just for Laughs (hahaha.com) holds the festival-scale slot. SoulPancake (soulpancake.com) is the touring-comedy peer. Stand Up NY (standupny.com) is the room precedent. We sit smaller, sharper on the close.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A touring-show operator built around 60-minute sets ending on the line.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Buys a ticket for a specific comic, not a venue. Wants to be in and out in 75 minutes. Doesn't drink during the show.

dos: Print the start and end time on the ticket
End the set on the line
Show the comic and the time

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only — Mic Drop Co. set in a single-weight grotesk, with a small black circle (the dropped mic head) below the word. The circle alone is the favicon.

typography.primary: Neue Haas Grotesk for the wordmark
typography.secondary: Neue Haas Grotesk Mono for showtimes
typography.rationale: One family. The mono carries the time, the regular carries the company.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Crowd work is the stand-up term for the improvised, audience-driven portion of a set — the segment where the comic talks to the front row. Naming the brand for the craft puts the improvised exchange at the center.
Corporate.industrySummary: Corporate-feeling comedy operators run touring shows, branded specials, and franchised rooms. There is room for an operator built around crowd-work tours and corporate-event bookings, with a managed roster of comics specializing in the form.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Live Nation Comedy (livenationcomedy.com) holds the institutional touring peer. CAA Comedy (caa.com) plays the talent-agency slot. Outback Presents (outbackpresents.com) sits in the touring-promoter middle. We sit smaller, focused on crowd-work specialists.
Corporate.positioningStatement: A touring operator and corporate booker for crowd-work specialists.

targetAudience.primary: Corporate event planners, college-circuit bookers, and theater operators booking touring stand-up.
behaviors: Manages a roster of specialist comics

dos: Speak to the booker, not the audience
donts: Photograph the comic in the green room

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a hallmark — Crowd Work Club set in a clean grotesk, paired with three small dot marks suggesting front-row chairs.

typography.primary: Inter for the wordmark and contracts
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed riders and tour books
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across decks. The serif handles printed riders.

Creative.brandNameRationale: The tight five is the working comic's calling card — five minutes of polished material, the unit booked for talk-show appearances and showcase auditions. Naming the room for the unit of measure puts the working comic's craft at the front.
Creative.industrySummary: There is space for a small creative venue built explicitly around the showcase format: ten comics, five minutes each, two nights a week, recorded for a YouTube clip.
Creative.competitorLandscape: UCB (ucbtheatre.com) holds the long-form improv peer slot. The Bell House (thebellhouseny.com) plays the showcase-venue precedent. The Pleasance (pleasance.co.uk) is the European fringe peer. We sit closer to The Bell House, sharper on the five-minute format.
Creative.positioningStatement: A creative showcase room running ten comics × five minutes, two nights a week.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 35. Watches stand-up clips on YouTube. Goes to a showcase once a month. Will line up an hour early for the front row.
behaviors: Watches clips before going to the show
Lines up for the front row
Posts the bit on the way home

dos: Show the ten names and the order
Record the night for the clip
Print the time per comic on the door

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark with a numeric mark — Tight Five set in a hand-drawn brush face, with a large stencil 5 as the favicon. The 5 is the favicon, the door sign, and the merch.

typography.primary: A brush face for the wordmark
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for time slots and order
typography.rationale: The brush face carries the showcase voice. The mono carries the running order.
